sheet.content:
## Key definitions
- **Logical (IP) and physical (MAC) addressing**: Logical addresses are 32-bit (IPv4) for network layer, physical addresses are 48-bit for data link layer [p. 1]
- **Store-and-forward packet switching**: Hosts send packets to nearest router, router stores packet until complete, then forwards [p. 1]
- **Services provided to the transport layer**: Independent of router technology, hides router number and topology, uses uniform address numbering [p. 1]
- **Routing algorithms**: Decide output line for incoming packet, optimality principle: if router J is on optimal path from I to K, then J to K follows same route [p. 1]
- **Congestion control**: Manages network congestion, causes: packets needing same output line, slow processors, insufficient buffer memory, low bandwidth lines [p. 2]

## Diagrams to draw
- **Routing algorithm**: Network as graph, routers as nodes, links as edges with cost (distance, delay) [p. 1]
- **Dijkstra's algorithm**: Source node marked permanent, neighbors labeled with tentative distance, repeated until destination marked permanent [p. 1]
- **Distance vector routing**: Network drawn as graph, routers as nodes, links as edges with cost, link state packet flooded to all routers, shortest paths computed with Dijkstra [p. 1]

## Formulas and code
None in this unit

## Must remember
- **Logical and physical addressing**: IP address 32-bit, MAC address 48-bit [p. 1]
- **Store-and-forward packet switching**: Hosts send packets to nearest router, router stores until complete, then forwards [p. 1]
- **Routing algorithms**: Dijkstra's algorithm, shortest path routing [p. 1]
- **Congestion control**: Leaky bucket algorithm, hosts have finite queue [p. 2]
- **IPv4 addressing**: 32-bit, 4.3 billion addresses, 128-bit for IPv6, 128-bit addresses practically unlimited [p. 2]
